newsitem.title: UK: Gene therapy still a way off - Genzyme VP.
newsitem.headline: Gene therapy still a way off - Genzyme VP.

text.p: Gene therapy is still in its infancy and faces too many hurdles to offer any immediate hope to patients, Alan Smith, Senior Vice President of Research at Genzyme Corp, said on Wednesday.
Smith said proper vectors had not been developed, scientists could not even identify target genes in many cases and it was still not clear how the body responded to efforts to introduced altered DNA.
"It is important to manage expectations about gene therapy," he told a conference in London. "Widespread, pivotal clinical trials are unlikely in the near future."
Smith said more work was needed on vectors, which carry the altered genetic material to the target cells.
"The vectors work pretty well," Smith, whose company is working with both viral and lipid vectors, said. "But I don't think they work well enough...As a drug they need to be more potent."

Then there was the problem of identifying where exactly to introduce the altered DNA. "In the case of cystic fibrosis...we are not even sure what the target is and we're not sure we can even get at it," he said.

Researchers were still facing obstacles from the body's immune response, although tinkering with the vectors could help with this problem, as could administering specific immune suppressants, Smith told the conference, sponsored by the Royal Society of Chemistry.

For example, in mice cytokines and neutrophils showed up very quickly after introduction of a vector. "We and others are trying to understand the molecular basis of such action. It looks like inflammation is mediated by the presence of lipid on the epithelial cells."
Smith said Genzyme had identified one "novel immune suppressant" that seemed to help -- deoxyspergualin or DSG. He said it affected CTL reponse in mice.
"We can see a longer duration of expression and we can repeat the dose," he said.
In addition, researchers were forced to work with very ill patients in whom it was hard to measure success. This was especially true of cancer patients.
"Clinical endpoints are, frankly, poor," Smith said. But, he concluded: "I believe this field has great promise for contributions in the next century."
